rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bilqis wisely tests whether Solomon is a worldly king satisfied by wealth or a prophet who will refuse it and require faith and submission.
rows.anchor: هذا من حسن نظرها وتدبيرها أي إني أجرب هذا الرجل بهدية

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, reports that Bilqis sent Solomon a brick of gold; seeing his gold walls made the envoys' gift seem small.
rows.anchor: فقال سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس: أرسلت إليه بلبنة من ذهب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Bilqis sent two hundred boys and two hundred girls.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: أرسلت إليه بمائتي غلام ومائتي جارية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas describes twelve girls disguised as boys, twelve boys as girls, musk and amber trays, gold-bearing mounts, two unusual beads, an empty cup, and a royal staff.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس: باثنتي عشرة وصيفة مذكرين قد ألبستهم زي الغلمان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One account says a single envoy carried the gift, accompanied by attendants and servants.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان الرسول واحدا ولكن كان في صحبته أتباع وخدم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account names the envoy as the noble al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr and says Bilqis sent one hundred boys and girls dressed in exchanged clothing, instructing them to speak in gender-disguised ways.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أرسلت رجلا من أشراف قومها يقال له المنذر بن عمرو

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: In the same account, the hoopoe told Solomon about the envoy's clothing and speech; an alternative says God informed Solomon.
rows.anchor: فيقال: إن الهدهد جاء وأخبر سليمان بذلك كله. وقيل: إن الله أخبر سليمان بذلك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Solomon staged a vast display: gold and silver paving, exotic sea creatures, thousands of seats for prophets and scholars, and ranks of people, jinn, and animals; the envoys were awed and discarded their gifts.
rows.anchor: فأمر سليمان عليه السلام أن يبسط من موضعه إلى تسع فراسخ بلبنات الذهب والفضة

rows.speaker: بعض الروايات
rows.claim: A variant says Solomon left a gift-sized unpaved strip; the envoys dropped their presents there to avoid suspicion, then feared the demons but were escorted through the ranks.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الروايات: إن سليمان لما أمرهم بفرش الميدان بلبنات الذهب والفضة

rows.speaker: بلقيس
rows.claim: Bilqis told her messenger that an angry look would mark Solomon as a king, while a cheerful, gentle look would identify a prophet whose words he should understand and answer.
rows.anchor: وكانت قالت لرسولها: إن نظر إليك نظر مغضب فاعلم أنه ملك

rows.speaker: بلقيس
rows.claim: Bilqis sent a gold box with an unpierced pearl and crookedly pierced bead, challenging Solomon to identify the attendants' sexes, box contents, staff ends, pierce and thread the objects, and fill a cup with dew.
rows.anchor: وكتبت كتابا مع رسولها تقول فيه: إن كنت نبيا فميز بين الوصفاء والوصائف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the envoy arrived, Gabriel informed Solomon what was inside the box, and Solomon told the envoy.
rows.anchor: فحركها، فأخبره جبريل بما فيها، ثم أخبرهم سليمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A termite carried a hair through the pearl's hole; Solomon granted its request to make its food come from trees.
rows.anchor: فجاءت الأرضة فأخذت شعرة في فيها حتى خرجت من الجانب الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A white worm threaded the crooked bead and asked Solomon to make fruit its food; he agreed.
rows.anchor: فقالت دودة بيضاء: أنا لها يا نبي الله فأخذت الدودة الخيط في فيها

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Solomon distinguished the boys and girls by their different ways of performing ablution.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: أمرهم بالوضوء، فجعل الرجل يحدر الماء على اليد والرجل حدرا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other descriptions distinguish them by how they take water, which hand they use, and whether they wash the palm-side or back of the forearm.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانت الجارية تأخذ الماء من الآنية بإحدى يديها، ثم تحملها على الأخرى

rows.speaker: يعلى بن مسلم عن سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says Bilqis sent two hundred attendants; starting ablution at the elbow marked females and at the palm marked males, while a thrown staff revealed its base by whichever end reached ground first.
rows.anchor: وروى يعلى بن مسلم عن سعيد بن جبير قال: أرسلت بلقيس بمائتي وصيفة ووصيف

rows.speaker: يعلى بن مسلم عن سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: In that report, Solomon ran horses until they sweated, filled the cup with their sweat, returned the gift, and Bilqis concluded that this was a matter from heaven.
rows.anchor: وأمر بالخيل فأجريت حتى عرقت وملأ القدح من عرقها، ثم رد سليمان الهدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet accepted and honored gifts but not charity; Solomon and the other prophets did likewise.
rows.anchor: كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يقبل الهدية ويثبت عليها ولا يقبل الصدقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bilqis used acceptance as a test because Solomon demanded submission; a gift could not ransom that demand, and using it to buy truth would be forbidden bribery.
rows.anchor: وإنما هي رشوة وبيع الحق بالباطل، وهي الرشوة التي لا تحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A freely given gift for affection and connection is generally lawful, but the author qualifies this rule when the giver is a polytheist.
rows.anchor: وأما الهدية المطلقة للتحبب والتواصل فإنها جائزة من كل أحد وعلى كل حال

rows.speaker: جماعة من العلماء
rows.claim: One hadith prohibits accepting polytheist support and gifts, while a report attributed to Malik from Thawr ibn Zayd says the Prophet accepted a gift; some scholars treated the reports as abrogating one another.
rows.anchor: في الحديث: " نهيت عن زبد المشركين " يعني رفدهم وعطاياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers reconciling the reports: gifts are refused from those hoping to defeat the Muslims, take their land, or enter Islam by that means, as with Solomon's situation.
rows.anchor: وهذا أحسن تأويل للعلماء في هذا فإنه جمع بين الأحاديث

rows.speaker: مالك عن عطاء بن عبد الله الخراساني
rows.claim: A report attributed through Malik to ʿAta al-Khurasani says handshakes remove rancor and gifts create affection and remove hostility.
rows.anchor: روى مالك عن عطاء بن عبد الله الخراساني قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: معاوية بن الحكم
rows.claim: Muʿawiya ibn al-Hakam says he heard the Prophet commend gift-giving as strengthening affection and removing inner rancor; al-Daraqutni calls its transmission singular and unreliable, and says it is not sound from Malik or al-Zuhri.
rows.anchor: وقال الدارقطني: تفرد به ابن بجير عن أبيه عن مالك، ولم يكن بالرضى

rows.speaker: ابن شهاب
rows.claim: Ibn Shihab reports that it reached him that the Prophet urged people to exchange gifts because gifts remove rancor.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن شهاب قال: بلغنا أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Other scholars held that the conflicting reports do not involve abrogation.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون ليس فيها ناسخ ولا منسوخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says people sitting with someone share in a gift, and scholars differ over what that sharing means.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: " جلساؤكم شركاؤكم في الهدية "

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the companions' share literally; another treats sharing as generosity and good manners, without a right to compel the recipient.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يشاركهم على وجه الكرم والمروءة، فإن لم يفعل فلا يجبر عليه

rows.speaker: أبو يوسف
rows.claim: Abu Yusuf limits the companions' share to fruit and similar foods.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو يوسف: ذلك في الفواكه ونحوها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say companions share the happiness occasioned by the gift, not the gift itself.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: هم شركاؤه في السرور لا في الهدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report applies to groups such as the People of the Bench and residents of lodges or hospices; a scholar given a gift specifically is not required to share, though sharing is generous.
rows.anchor: أما إذا كان فقيها من الفقهاء اختص بها فلا شركة فيها لأصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here فناظرة means waiting or expecting.
rows.anchor: أي منتظرة { بم يرجع المرسلون } قال قتادة: يرحمها الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada praises Bilqis as discerning in both Islam and polytheism, since she knew gifts have an effect on people.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: يرحمها الله أن كانت لعاقلة في إسلامها وشركها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif is omitted in بما to distinguish it from declarative ما; retaining it is also permissible.
rows.anchor: وسقطت الألف في { بم } للفرق بين «ما» الخبرية. وقد يجوز إثباتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited line demonstrates the permissible written alif in على ما.
rows.anchor: على ما قام يشتمني لئيم كخنزير تمرغ في رماد

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yunus explains that السخيمة means rancor.
rows.anchor: قال ابن وهب: سألت يونس عن السخيمة ما هي فقال: الغل

rows.speaker: عثمان الوقاصي
rows.claim: The route through ʿUthman al-Waqqasi from al-Zuhri is weak.
rows.anchor: وهذا الحديث وصله الوقاصي عثمان عن الزهري وهو ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's acceptance of gifts is established and exemplary; gifts remove inner resentments and make encounters more gracious.
rows.anchor: وعلى الجملة: فقد ثبت أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يقبل الهدية

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet says mutual gifts generate connection, affection, and pleasant social presence.
rows.anchor: هدايا الناس بعضهم لبعض تولد في قلوبهم الوصالا

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: A second unnamed poet says gifts are valued even more than a child by a fond parent.
rows.anchor: إن الهدايا لها حظ إذا وردت أحظى من الابن عند الوالد الحدب

rows.speaker: حمزة ويعقوب والأعمش
rows.claim: Hamza, Yaʿqub, and al-Aʿmash read أتمدونني with one doubled nūn and a following yāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة ويعقوب والأعمش: بنون واحدة مشددة وياء ثابتة بعدها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: The remaining readers use two nūns; Abu ʿUbayd prefers this reading because all codices write two nūns.
rows.anchor: الباقون بنونين وهو اختيار أبي عبيد لأنها في كل المصاحف بنونين

rows.speaker: إسحاق عن نافع
rows.claim: Ishaq reports Nafiʿ reading one light nūn followed in pronunciation by yāʾ; Ibn al-Anbari says the yāʾ should be retained at pause to match the codex spelling.
rows.anchor: وقد روى إسحاق عن نافع أنه كان يقرأ: { أتمدون } بنون واحدة مخففة بعدها ياء في اللفظ

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari explains the light nūn as reduction of an underlying doubled nūn, analogous to other Arabic contractions.
rows.anchor: والأصل في النون التشديد، فخفف التشديد من ذا الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary supports the contraction with Arabic forms such as يضربون and a poetic shortening of ترهبيني to ترهبين.
rows.anchor: والأصل ترهبيني فخفف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon asks whether they are adding wealth to what they already see of his possessions.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { أتمدونني } أتزيدونني مالا إلى ما تشاهدونه من أموالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's gifts of Islam, kingship, and prophethood are better than what the envoys brought, so Solomon does not rejoice in wealth.
rows.anchor: أي فما أعطاني من الإسلام والملك والنبوة خير مما أعطاكم

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ونافع وحفص
rows.claim: Although all codices omit the yāʾ in آتاني, Abu ʿAmr, Nafiʿ, and Hafs read it with an open yāʾ and drop it at pause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو ونافع وحفص: { آتاني الله } بياء مفتوحة فإذا وقفوا حذفوا

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqub keeps the yāʾ when pausing but drops it in connected reading to avoid meeting two vowelless letters.
rows.anchor: وأما يعقوب فإنه يثبتها في الوقف ويحذف في الوصل لالتقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The other readers omit the yāʾ both in pause and in connected reading.
rows.anchor: الباقون بغير ياء في الحالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon says the envoys rejoice in their gift because they are people who boast and compete in worldly things.
rows.anchor: لأنكم أهل مفاخرة ومكاثرة في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon's order to return is addressed to al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr, the delegation's commander.
rows.anchor: أي قال سليمان للمنذر بن عمرو أمير الوفد ارجع إليهم بهديتهم

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن بن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan calls the lām an emphatic lām and classifies Arabic lām particles as emphasis, command, and genitive; the oath lām entails the nūn.
rows.anchor: وسمعت أبا الحسن بن كيسان يقول: هي لام توكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لا قبل لهم بها means they have no strength or capacity to face the army.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { لا قبل لهم بها } أي لا طاقة لهم عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: منها refers to their land; an alternative identifies it as the town of Sheba mentioned earlier.
rows.anchor: { ولنخرجنهم منها } أي من أرضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will be stripped of their kingdom and honor and made humiliated unless they submit to Islam.
rows.anchor: قد سلبوا ملكهم وعزهم. { وهم صاغرون } أي مهانون أذلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the envoy reported what he saw, Bilqis recognized that Solomon was no ordinary king and that her people could not fight a prophet; she hid her throne in nested chambers and traveled with twelve thousand Yemeni lords, each commanding one hundred thousand.
rows.anchor: فقالت: قد عرفت أنه ليس بملك ولا طاقة لنا بقتال نبي من أنبياء الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Solomon inspired such awe that he let no one begin a matter before he asked; seeing nearby dust, he asked what it was and was told Bilqis had arrived.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: وكان سليمان مهيبا لا يبتدأ بشيء حتى يكون هو الذي يسأل عنه

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes the reassurance not to grieve as referring to separation from Moses.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: لا تحزني لفراقه قاله ابن زيد

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Sallam says Moses' mother is told not to grieve that he might be killed.
rows.anchor: الثاني: لا تحزني أن يقتل قاله يحيى بن سلام

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Reports differ on how long she nursed Moses before placing him in a five-span box and casting it into the river: four months, three months, or eight months according to al-Kalbi's account.
rows.anchor: بعد أن أرضعته أربعة أشهر. وقال آخرون: ثلاثة أشهر. وقال آخرون ثمانية أشهر في حكاية الكلبي

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi recounts that the carpenter who made the box informed Pharaoh; God blinded him so he lost his way, recognized the feared child, and became the believer from Pharaoh's family.
rows.anchor: نم إلى فرعون بخبره، فبعث معه من يأخذه، فطمس الله عينيه وقلبه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Satan made Moses' mother regret her choice when the box disappeared; God reassured her that He would return him and make him a messenger to Egypt.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: فلما توارى عنها ندمها الشيطان

words: وأوحينا إلى أم موسى أن أرضعيه
rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asmaʿi praises an Arab girl's poem and notes that the verse combines two commands, two prohibitions, two statements, and two glad tidings.
rows.anchor: فقلت: قاتلك الله ما أفصحك! فقالت: أو يعد هذا فصاحة مع قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām marks consequence, not the family's intention: they took Moses hoping for joy, but the outcome was that he became their enemy and grief.
rows.anchor: فاللام في { ليكون } لام العاقبة ولام الصيرورة لأنهم إنما أخذوه ليكون لهم قرة عين

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet illustrates the consequence construction by saying that every nursing mother nurtures someone destined for death and every home is built for ruin.
rows.anchor: وللمنايا تربي كل مرضعة ودورنا لخراب الدهر نبنيها

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: A second unnamed poet likewise says mothers raise children for death and houses are built for destruction, demonstrating outcome rather than intent.
rows.anchor: فللموت تغدو الوالدات سخالها كما لخراب الدهر تبنى المساكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: التقاط is finding something without seeking or intending it; Arabic also uses the verb for an accidental encounter, and the legal discussion of found property was treated in Surat Yusuf.
rows.anchor: والالتقاط وجود الشيء من غير طلب ولا إرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poetic phrase منهلا وردته التقاطا illustrates an accidental finding; the word is also the source of luqata, lost property, whose rules were discussed in Surat Yusuf.
rows.anchor: ومنهل وردته التقاطا ومنه اللقطة. وقد مضى بيان ذلك من الأحكام

rows.speaker: الأعمش ويحيى والمفضل وحمزة والكسائي وخلف
rows.claim: These readers pronounce حزنًا with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on zāy; the remaining readers use fatḥa on both, which Abu ʿUbayd selects, and Abu Hatim favors emphatic pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش ويحيى والمفضل وحمزة والكسائي وخلف: { وحزنا } بضم الحاء وسكون الزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two pronunciations are dialectal forms, like the variant pairs for want, sickness, and right guidance.
rows.anchor: وهما لغتان مثل العدم والعدم، والسقم والسقم، والرشد والرشد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Haman was Pharaoh's minister and was a Copt.
rows.anchor: وكان وزيره من القبط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse calls Pharaoh, Haman, and their troops disobedient, polytheistic sinners.
rows.anchor: أي عاصين مشركين آثمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asiya saw the box floating, had it brought and opened, pitied the child, and asked Pharaoh to spare him as a delight to them.
rows.anchor: أن آسية امرأة فرعون رأت التابوت يعوم في البحر، فأمرت بسوقه إليها وفتحه

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi parses qurrata as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning this child is a delight to me and you.
rows.anchor: { قرة } خبر ابتداء مضمر قاله الكسائي

rows.speaker: النحاس عن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas reports Abu Ishaq's more remote analysis: qurrata is the subject and لا تقتلوه its predicate, meaning that because he is our delight, they should not kill him.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وفيه وجه آخر بعيد ذكره أبو إسحاق

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: An alternative places a pause after ولك; Ibn Masʿud's reading supports it by putting لا تقتلوه before قرة عين لي ولك.
rows.anchor: في قراءة عبد الله بن مسعود: { وقالت امرأة فرعون لا تقتلوه قرة عين لي ولك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative analysis treats the phrase as do not kill him, a delight to me and you.
rows.anchor: ويجوز النصب بمعنى لا تقتلوا قرة عين لي ولك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She uses the plural form to address Pharaoh in the manner of tyrants, who are addressed and speak of themselves in the plural.
rows.anchor: وقالت: { لا تقتلوه } ولم تقل لا تقتله فهي تخاطب فرعون كما يخاطب الجبارون

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An account says she urged mercy because the child came from another land and was not Israelite; she hoped he would benefit them or become their son, since she was childless, and Pharaoh gave him to her.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قالت: { لا تقتلوه } فإن الله أتى به من أرض أخرى وليس من بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's dream interpreters predicted an Israelite boy would ruin his kingdom, so he killed infants in alternating years; Aaron was born in a spared year and Moses in a slaughter year.
rows.anchor: فعاد يذبح عاما ويستحيي عاما، فولد هارون في عام الاستحياء، وولد موسى في عام الذبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first reading, God's words mean Pharaoh's people did not realize Moses would bring about their destruction.
rows.anchor: هذا ابتداء كلام من الله تعالى أي وهم لا يشعرون أن هلاكهم بسببه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Alternatively, the words belong to Pharaoh's wife: the Israelites did not know she had taken Moses in and thought he was her child.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو من كلام المرأة أي وبنو إسرائيل لا يدرون أنا التقطناه

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group places the exchange when Asiya opened the box; Pharaoh recognized an Israelite child and called for executioners, but she pleaded for the child, and Pharaoh said he was no delight to him.
rows.anchor: فقال: علي بالذباحين فقالت امرأته ما ذكر فقال فرعون: أما لي فلا

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: The cited verse of poetry describes the fearful commotion caused when someone came crying out for help.
rows.anchor: كنا إذا ما أتانا صارخ فزع كان الصراخ له قرع الظنابيب

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri identifies the Israelite who sought help as the Samaritan and says Pharaoh's cook had pressed him into carrying firewood to the kitchen.
rows.anchor: استسخره طباخ فرعون في حمل الحطب إلى المطبخ ذكره القشيري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الذي is nominative as the subject, with يستصرخه as its predicate; it can also be accusative as a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: { الذي } رفع بالابتداء و { يستصرخه } في موضع الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أمس means the day before; when unprefixed it is built on kasra for the meeting of two vowelless letters, but normally becomes declinable with the article or a possessive suffix.
rows.anchor: وأمس لليوم الذي قبل يومك، وهو مبني على الكسر لالتقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: سيبويه وغيره
rows.claim: Some Arabs keep أمس indeclinable even with the article in nominative position; poets may extend that treatment to genitive or accusative under poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: وحكى سيبويه وغيره أن من العرب من يجري أمس مجرى ما لا ينصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: غوي can mean ruined or unsuccessful, since Moses was challenging someone he could not withstand; another gloss is clearly misguided, because the Egyptian's conduct had brought a death yesterday and another threatened today.
rows.anchor: والغوي الخائب أي لأنك تشاد من لا تطيقه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says Moses called the Egyptian clearly misguided for exploiting the Israelite and preparing to strike him.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: إنما قال للقبطي: { إنك لغوي مبين } في استسخار هذا الإسرائيلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: غوي is an intensive form from أغوى, used in the sense of the causative participle; it may also mean one who has gone astray.
rows.anchor: والغوي فعيل من أغوى يغوي، وهو بمعنى مغو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb بطش has both a- and u-vowel forms; the u-vowel is more analogical because the verb is intransitive.
rows.anchor: يقال: بطش يبطش ويبطش والضم أقيس لأنه فعل لا يتعدى

words: أتريد أن تقتلني كما قتلت نفسا بالأمس
rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says Moses moved to strike the Egyptian, but the Israelite thought Moses meant him after the harsh rebuke; the Egyptian heard the words and spread them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جبير. أراد موسى أن يبطش بالقبطي فتوهم الإسرائيلي أنه يريده

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account says the Israelite was about to strike the Egyptian, Moses stopped him, and the frightened Israelite thought Moses meant to kill him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد أن يبطش الإسرائيلي بالقبطي فنهاه موسى فخاف منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إن تريد here means you want nothing except that.
rows.anchor: { إن تريد } أي ما تريد. { إلا أن تكون

rows.speaker: عكرمة والشعبي
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Shaʿbi define a tyrant here as someone who has killed two people unjustly.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة والشعبي: لا يكون الإنسان جبارا حتى يقتل نفسين بغير حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people meant by reformers are those who reconcile disputes between people.
rows.anchor: أي من الذين يصلحون بين الناس

rows.speaker: أكثر أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the man as Hezekiel ibn Sabura, the believer from Pharaoh's family and Pharaoh's cousin; al-Thaʿlabi records this view.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر أهل التفسير: هذا الرجل هو حزقيل بن صبورا مؤمن آل فرعون

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli identifies the man as Talut; al-Mahdawi reports Qatada's identification as Shamʿun, and another view gives the name Shamʿan.
rows.anchor: وقيل: طالوت ذكره السهيلي. وقال المهدوي عن قتادة: شمعون

rows.speaker: الدارقطني
rows.claim: Al-Daraqutni says the name Shamʿan, with šīn, is known only as the believer from Pharaoh's family.
rows.anchor: قال الدارقطني: لا يعرف شمعان بالشين المعجمة إلا مؤمن آل فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Pharaoh ordered Moses' execution, and the man hurried to warn him that the council was consulting about killing him for the Egyptian killed the previous day.
rows.anchor: وروي أن فرعون أمر بقتل موسى فسبق ذلك الرجل بالخبر

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari says يأتمرون can mean that the council consults together or that its members command one another; the same root appears in 65:6 and in al-Nimr ibn Tawlab's poetry.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري: ائتمر القوم وتآمروا أي أمر بعضهم بعضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: يترقب means watching for or expecting pursuit.
rows.anchor: أي ينتظر الطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asks God to rescue him from the unjust people.
rows.anchor: قال رب نجني من القوم الظالمين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A tyrant may mean one who beats and kills unjustly without considering consequences or choosing what is better, or an arrogant person who will not humble himself before God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الجبار الذي يفعل ما يريده من الضرب والقتل بظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses fled alone, afraid and without provisions, comfort, or shoes, toward Midian because of his kinship with its people; seeing his ignorance of the route and need, he entrusted himself to God for guidance.
rows.anchor: لما خرج موسى عليه السلام فارا بنفسه منفردا خائفا، لا شيء معه من زاد ولا راحة ولا حذاء نحو مدين

rows.speaker: أبو مالك
rows.claim: Abu Malik says Pharaoh sent searchers to the road passes, where Moses would be lost; an angel on horseback with a spear guided him and, it is said, gave him his staff.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مالك: وكان فرعون وجه في طلبه وقال لهم: اطلبوه في ثنيات الطريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says Moses took the staff in Midian for shepherding; the author says this account is more common and sounder.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن عصاه إنما أخذها لرعي الغنم من مدين. وهو أكثر وأصح

rows.speaker: مقاتل والسدي
rows.claim: Muqatil and al-Suddi say God sent Gabriel to Moses; the author leaves the truth to God.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل والسدي: إن الله بعث إليه جبريل فالله أعلم

rows.speaker: ابن جبير والناس
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr and others say the journey from Egypt to Midian took eight days, and Midian was ruled by someone other than Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: وبين مدين ومصر ثمانية أيام قاله ابن جبير والناس. وكان ملك مدين لغير فرعون

rows.speaker: أبو مالك
rows.claim: A report says Moses lived on leaves and reached Midian after the soles of his feet wore away.
rows.anchor: قلت: روي أنه كان يتقوت ورق الشجر، وما وصل حتى سقط خف قدميه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs Moses brought were manifest and clear; Pharaoh's people called them fabricated magic and said their ancestors had heard nothing like them.
rows.anchor: أي ظاهرات واضحات { قالوا ما هذا إلا سحر مفترى } مكذوب مختلق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say these signs were Moses' rational arguments for God's oneness; others say they were his miracles.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن هذه الآيات ما احتج به موسى في إثبات التوحيد من الحجج العقلية

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن كثير وابن محيصن
rows.claim: The common reading includes the conjunction و; Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, and Ibn Muhaysin read قال without it, as in the Meccan codex.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وابن كثير وابن محيصن: { قال } بلا واو وكذلك هو في مصحف أهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الهدى here means right guidance.
rows.anchor: أي بالرشاد

rows.speaker: الكوفيون إلا عاصما
rows.claim: All Kufan readers except Asim read يكون with yāʾ; the others read تكون with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ الكوفيون إلا عاصما: { يكون } بالياء والباقون بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عاقبة الدار means the abode of recompense.
rows.anchor: أي دار الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in إنه is the pronoun of the matter or affair.
rows.anchor: الهاء ضمير الأمر والشأن

words: ما علمت لكم من إله غيري
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says forty years separated Pharaoh's claim here from أنا ربكم الأعلى; Pharaoh lied, for he knew he had a Lord who created him and his people, as 43:87 confirms.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كان بينها وبين قوله:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the command as cooking bricks for Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: أي اطبخ لي الآجر عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Pharaoh was the first to make fired bricks and build with them.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هو أول من صنع الآجر وبنى به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Haman gathered fifty thousand builders, apart from support workers, and ordered bricks and plaster baked, timber cut, and nails made; the structure rose beyond any previous building.
rows.anchor: جمع هامان العمال قيل خمسين ألف بناء سوى الأتباع والأجراء

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Pharaoh climbed the structure and shot an arrow skyward; when it returned stained with blood, Pharaoh claimed to have killed Moses' god.
rows.anchor: فحكى السدي: أن فرعون صعد السطح ورمى بنشابة نحو السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Gabriel struck the tower with his wing, splitting it into three pieces that fell on the army, into the sea, and westward; the author questions the report's reliability.
rows.anchor: فروي أن جبريل عليه السلام بعثه الله تعالى عند مقالته، فضرب الصرح بجناحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ظن here means doubt; Pharaoh disbelieved while doubting, despite proofs so evident that a sound nature would not be deceived by them.
rows.anchor: الظن هنا شك، فكفر على الشك لأنه قد رأى من البراهين ما لا يخيل على ذي فطرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: استكبر means acted arrogantly; Pharaoh and his troops set themselves above belief in Moses.
rows.anchor: أي تعظم { هو وجنوده } أي عن الإيمان بموسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their arrogance was wrongful aggression: they had no proof that could answer what Moses brought.
rows.anchor: أي بالعدوان، أي لم تكن له حجة تدفع ما جاء به موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They imagined there would be no return to God, resurrection, or afterlife.
rows.anchor: أي توهموا أنه لا معاد ولا بعث

rows.speaker: نافع وابن محيصن وشيبة وحميد ويعقوب وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers use the active form لا يرجعون; the remaining readers use the passive form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن محيصن وشيبة وحميد ويعقوب وحمزة والكسائي: { لا يرجعون }

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد وأبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayd selects the passive reading, while Abu Hatim selects the active reading.
rows.anchor: وهو اختيار أبي عبيد، والأول اختيار أبي حاتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The army numbered two million six hundred thousand; God cast Pharaoh and his troops into the salt sea.
rows.anchor: وكانوا ألفي ألف وستمائة ألف. { فنبذناهم في اليم }
